messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sameer describes his life before the attack as one defined by color and light. A painter by trade, his days were spent in his studio in his home city, a place he had lived for all of his 51 years. That life ended two years ago, the day an artillery shell struck the apartment building next to his. The blast threw him across his studio, pinning him under a collapsed section of drywall. For what felt like an eternity, he lay there, his body contorted, the air thick with the acrid smell of plaster dust and burning rubber from the street below. He could hear the screams, the chaos, and the terrible finality of the silence that followed, but he was powerless, trapped in a position he felt his body would never forget.

Now, living in the United States with his wife, the war is geographically distant but psychically immediate. The world Sameer inhabits is a minefield of sensory cues that detonate the past. The sharp scent of turpentine in his new, sterile studio can suddenly mingle with the ghost of burning rubber, and in an instant, he is no longer in his workshop but back on the floor, helpless. A car backfiring on the street outside doesn't just make him jump; it sends a jolt of pure terror through him, his body tensing as if anticipating an impact. Each unexpected sound serves as fresh evidence for a conclusion he has already reached: that nowhere is truly safe, and that the quiet of his new life is merely a fragile illusion. This constant state of being on guard has left him perpetually exhausted, his muscles knotted with a tension that never fully subsides. He feels this hypervigilance is the only thing keeping him safe, a necessary shield against a world he has come to believe is fundamentally and irrevocably dangerous. This belief makes him scan every doorway and watch every stranger, priming his senses for the next inevitable threat.

When a trigger, be it a sudden bang or an unexpected smell, breaks through his defenses, the memory is not a simple recollection. It is a full-body reenactment. He feels the phantom weight on his legs, his shoulders instinctively hunching into the same cramped position he held under the debris. With this physical reliving comes a wave of overwhelming grief for his neighbors, for his city, for the man he used to be. The memory itself feels fractured and unreal, so horrific that part of his mind struggles to accept it ever happened, yet his body remembers it with perfect, agonizing fidelity. After the memory breaks through, the threat feels immediate and physical—not something that happened in the past, but something that is still happening to him in the present. The flashback leaves him standing in his own studio feeling hunted and exposed, certain that the collapse could happen again, right here, right now. To prevent this unbearable physical re-experiencing, he has learned that he must keep his mind and body in constant motion; stillness is the enemy that allows the past to rush in. This profound sense of loss and the physical horror of the memory reinforce his certainty that he is broken beyond repair. The memory proves the world is dangerous; his body's reaction proves he is no longer capable of living in it.

This conviction that he is no longer the man he was—that the part of him that could create, that could feel safe, has been permanently destroyed—governs his days. This belief that he is irreparably damaged seems to call the memory forward, as if his mind is constantly searching for the exact moment he was shattered, replaying the evidence of his own ruin. The joy he once found in his art now feels meaningless, a frivolous activity from a past life. Believing he is no longer capable of painting, he instead throws himself into "keeping busy." He spends hours in his studio organizing brushes, prepping canvases, and sanding frames, performing the labor of an artist without ever touching paint to canvas. This frantic activity is a desperate attempt to outrun his thoughts and the constant, low-grade alertness humming through his veins. At night, when the busyness stops, his mind circles endlessly around the same question: why him? Why was his building spared and not the one next door? This rumination offers no answers, only cementing the feeling that he is adrift in a chaotic, hostile world where nothing makes sense.

The feedback loop has become unbearable. His attempts to manage his state, primarily through distraction and avoiding any news that might mention conflict, only seem to make him more sensitive. The very effort of constantly pushing the past away has, paradoxically, kept it vivid and close; by refusing to examine it, he has ensured the memory remains unprocessed and potent, ready to ambush him. The constant tension makes him startle more easily, which in turn brings back the memories with greater force. The memories confirm his darkest beliefs about himself and the world, which then fuels his need to stay busy and avoidant, preventing any real processing from occurring. His wife’s attempts to connect are often rebuffed; he has to leave the room if the evening news comes on, creating a painful distance between them. The final straw came last week when, urged by his wife, he tried to paint. The moment he opened the mineral spirits, the smell triggered a flashback so intense he simply froze, brush in hand, until she found him an hour later, staring blankly at the wall. It was the starkest evidence yet of what he had lost. He has come to therapy not with a clear hope, but with a quiet, desperate plea: to find some meaning in the wreckage, and to one day be able to pick up a brush without his own body betraying him.
